title: Paddington in Peru
author: VirtueVigil Editorial Team

wokeTrap.explanation: Paddington in Peru is not a woke trap. The Paddington franchise has always been a genuine family adventure series about a well-mannered, marmalade-loving bear from Peru adopted by a London family. The third installment continues this tradition without any bait-and-switch. What you see in the trailers is what you get: a charming adventure about family, identity, and belonging. There's no hidden agenda, no lecture, no surprise ideological payload. Some critics have tried to read the Paddington franchise as an immigration allegory, and the subtext is certainly there if you squint, but the films themselves never weaponize it. Paddington is not coded as a political statement. He's coded as a good bear.

woke_trap_assessment.explanation: Not a woke trap. The Paddington franchise has been consistent since 2014 in what it offers: warm, gentle, family-friendly adventure centered on kindness, good manners, and the importance of chosen family. Paddington in Peru continues this pattern faithfully. While immigration subtext exists in the franchise DNA (a bear from Peru finds a home with a British family), the films never lecture about it. They simply tell a good story and let the themes emerge naturally. No family walking into this film will encounter anything they didn't expect.

director.name: Dougal Wilson
director.ideology: UNKNOWN/NEUTRAL. First-time feature director with background in commercials and music videos. No public political statements or ideological track record to assess.
director.profile: Dougal Wilson is a British director known primarily for his acclaimed advertising work, including beloved John Lewis Christmas adverts, and music videos for artists like Coldplay and Bat for Lashes. Paddington in Peru is his feature film debut. Wilson was chosen to replace Paul King, who directed the first two Paddington films to near-universal acclaim (97% and 99% on Rotten Tomatoes respectively). Wilson brings a visual sensibility honed by years of commercial work, and it shows: the film is gorgeous, with vivid Peruvian landscapes and inventive set pieces. What he lacks compared to King is the razor-sharp comedic timing and the ability to make every single scene feel essential. The film occasionally wanders in its midsection in a way the first two never did. But Wilson proves himself a capable steward of the franchise, and his instinct for emotional sincerity is genuine.

writer.name: Mark Burton, Jon Foster, James Lamont
writer.profile: Mark Burton co-wrote the screenplays for all three Paddington films (alongside Paul King for the first two). Jon Foster and James Lamont are British comedy writers who have worked together on shows like The Tracey Ullman Show and the animated film Gnomeo & Juliet. The story was developed by Paul King, Simon Farnaby, and Mark Burton, ensuring continuity with the franchise's creative DNA. The screenplay draws inspiration from Werner Herzog's Aguirre, the Wrath of God and Fitzcarraldo for its Peruvian jungle adventure sequences. The script's strongest elements are its villain work (Olivia Colman's Reverend Mother reveal is delicious) and its emotional core (Paddington's connection to his origins). Its weakest element is pacing: the middle act sags under the weight of an overly complicated treasure hunt plot.

fidelityCasting.assessment: Paddington in Peru handles its casting reasonably well but not flawlessly. The core Brown family is intact from prior films, with the notable exception of Emily Mortimer replacing Sally Hawkins as Mary Brown. Hawkins chose not to return for personal reasons, and Mortimer slides into the role with grace, though longtime fans will notice the swap. The Peruvian setting raises the most obvious casting question: the film is set entirely in Peru but features very few Peruvian or Latin American actors in prominent roles. Antonio Banderas (Spanish, not Peruvian) plays the riverboat captain, and Carla Tous (Colombian) plays his daughter. Common Sense Media specifically flagged the lack of notable Peruvian actors. That said, the film's central character is literally a Peruvian bear voiced by a British actor, so the franchise has never claimed to be a showcase for Peruvian representation. The casting is serviceable and star-driven, not ideologically motivated in either direction.
details: Emily Mortimer replaces Sally Hawkins as Mary Brown. Smooth transition, though Hawkins is missed.
Antonio Banderas is Spanish, not Peruvian, playing a character in Peru. Standard Hollywood casting.
Carla Tous is Colombian, replacing Rachel Zegler who left due to the SAG-AFTRA strike.
No major Peruvian actors in the cast despite the Peruvian setting.
Imelda Staunton continues to voice Aunt Lucy, a Peruvian bear, with a British accent. Consistent with franchise logic.

summary.overall:
# Paddington in Peru (2025)

**Classification: MIXED (Leaning Traditional)**

**WOKE 8.4 | TRADITIONAL 22.5 | Composite +14 TRAD**

**Confidence: HIGH**

---

## Opening Hook

Paddington Bear has become one of the strangest cultural Rorschach tests in modern cinema. Progressives see him as an immigration parable: a brown-skinned refugee from a developing nation, taken in by a white British family, who proves his worth through politeness and hard work. Conservatives claimed him after Queen Elizabeth herself shared tea and marmalade sandwiches with the little bear in that 2022 Platinum Jubilee sketch, cementing Paddington as an icon of traditional British values, good manners, and institutional respect. Both readings have some truth. Neither captures the full picture.

Paddington in Peru, the third film in the franchise, sidesteps the debate entirely by doing what Paddington does best: being kind, being funny, and making you feel things. Director Dougal Wilson, stepping in for Paul King (who directed the first two films to 97% and 99% on Rotten Tomatoes), delivers a perfectly pleasant adventure that families will enjoy and forget within a week. It's charming. It's warm. It's also the weakest entry in the franchise by a meaningful margin, and the reasons have nothing to do with politics.

---

## Plot Summary

Paddington receives a letter from the Home for Retired Bears in Peru informing him that his beloved Aunt Lucy misses him terribly and has been acting strangely. Paddington and the entire Brown family (Henry, Mary, Judy, Jonathan, Mrs. Bird, and Mr. Gruber) pack up and head to Peru to visit her.

When they arrive at the convent where Aunt Lucy lives, the Reverend Mother (Olivia Colman, doing what Olivia Colman does, which is steal every scene she enters) informs them that Lucy has disappeared into the jungle, leaving behind only her glasses and a bracelet. Paddington discovers a map in Lucy's cabin pointing toward a mysterious place called Rumi Rock.

The Browns hire a riverboat captain named Hunter Cabot (Antonio Banderas) and his daughter Gina (Carla Tous) to take them downriver. Hunter, it turns out, is obsessed with finding El Dorado, the legendary lost city of gold, and sees Paddington's bracelet as the key to unlocking its location. Hunter's treasure fever eventually causes a shipwreck and separates Paddington from the family.

Meanwhile, Mrs. Bird grows suspicious of the Reverend Mother back at the convent and discovers she's actually Clarissa Cabot, Hunter's supposedly dead cousin, who staged Lucy's disappearance to lure Paddington to Peru so she could use his bracelet to find El Dorado herself.

The threads converge at an ancient Incan fortress where Clarissa reveals her true identity, holds the family at gunpoint, and is ultimately stopped by Hunter, who finally overcomes his gold obsession and chooses family over fortune. The Browns use Paddington's bracelet to enter El Dorado, which turns out not to be a city of gold but an orangery, a hidden grove where Paddington was born and where bears have been making marmalade for generations. Lucy is safe. Paddington reconnects with his origins, bonds with the other bears, and then makes the choice to return to London with the Browns. Home isn't where you're from. It's where your family is.

Hugh Grant pops up in a post-credits scene, reprising his role as the wonderfully hammy Phoenix Buchanan from Paddington 2, delivering a perfect little comedy coda.

## Culture War Discourse

Paddington has occupied an unusual position in the culture war since the first film dropped in 2014. Early on, some right-leaning commentators flagged the original as "anti-UKIP propaganda" for its sympathetic portrayal of a foreign bear being welcomed into Britain. Then Queen Elizabeth did the Jubilee sketch with Paddington, and suddenly conservatives were claiming him as an icon of traditionalism and British values. Paddington became politically uncancellable from both directions.

Paddington in Peru generates almost zero culture war heat on its own. Worth It or Woke, a conservative review site, rated it positively and specifically praised the fact that "in a shocking and beyond-refreshing turn of events, there's nothing to report" on the parental content front. They noted the dad is "mildly prissy but mans up and saves the day," the riverboat captain wrestles with a character flaw, and the son learns the value of hard work. All traditional arc structures.

The only cultural friction point is the casting of non-Peruvian actors in a Peru-set film. Common Sense Media flagged it. But this is a franchise where a British actor voices a Peruvian bear who lives with a London family, so demanding geographic casting accuracy feels like looking for a fight where there isn't one.

The honest assessment: Paddington in Peru is one of those rare modern films that both progressives and conservatives can watch without reaching for their phones to complain. It's wholesome. It's clean. It's apolitical in practice, even if you can construct political readings if you try hard enough.

---

## Comparison to Prior Paddington Films

The first Paddington (2014) was a revelation. Nobody expected a live-action/CGI children's film about a talking bear to be one of the best comedies of the decade. Paul King's direction was inventive, the humor was sophisticated without being exclusionary, and the emotional beats landed with precision. Rotten Tomatoes: 97%.

Paddington 2 (2017) somehow improved on the original. For a stretch, it held the all-time record on Rotten Tomatoes at 100% before settling at 99%. Hugh Grant's Phoenix Buchanan was one of the great comic villains of the decade. The prison sequence was inspired. The film proved that a franchise could grow without losing its soul.

Paddington in Peru is a good film. It is not a great film. The transition from Paul King to Dougal Wilson is noticeable. Wilson has a strong visual eye (his background in commercials and music videos shows in the gorgeous Peruvian cinematography), but he lacks King's gift for perfectly calibrated comedy and his ability to make every scene feel essential. The midsection sags. The treasure hunt plot is more convoluted than it needs to be. The villain reveal, while entertaining (Olivia Colman is incapable of being boring), lacks the sustained comic genius of Hugh Grant's Buchanan.

The emotional core holds. Paddington's choice to return to London with the Browns after reconnecting with his birth origins is genuinely moving. The film understands what it's about: home is where love is, not where blood is. That's a traditional message delivered with sincerity, and it works.

But the magic is diluted. Paddington 1 and 2 were films you told your friends about because they were shockingly good. Paddington in Peru is a film you take your kids to because it's perfectly safe and reasonably entertaining. That's a meaningful gap.

---

## Adult Viewer Insight

Conservative parents can take their kids to this without a single concern. There's no agenda. There's no lecture. The male characters have genuine arcs. Henry Brown starts the film as an anxious, slightly bumbling dad and steps up when his family needs him. Hunter Cabot overcomes greed and chooses his daughter over gold. Jonathan Brown learns the value of hard work. These aren't revolutionary character beats, but they're traditionally coded and sincerely executed.

The women are also well-served. Mary Brown is warm, competent, and central to the family's emotional life. Mrs. Bird is tough, observant, and the one who uncovers the villain's plot. Olivia Colman's villain is funny and menacing without being an ideological statement about female empowerment or villainy.

The immigration subtext is present if you look for it (a bear who left Peru and must decide whether to stay or return), but the film never foregrounds it or turns it into a speech. It's texture, not thesis.

For conservative viewers: this is one of the cleanest, most family-friendly theatrical releases you'll see in 2025. Enjoy it.

---

## Parental Guidance

**Recommended minimum age: 5+**

Paddington in Peru is rated PG and earns that rating honestly.

**Content Breakdown:**

- **Violence (Mild):** Some peril and action sequences during the jungle adventure. A shipwreck scene. The villain holds characters at gunpoint briefly. Nothing graphic, nothing scary for kids over 5.
- **Language (None):** Clean throughout. No profanity.
- **Sexual Content (None):** Nothing. Zero. A perfectly clean film.
- **Frightening Scenes (Mild):** Some jungle animals and a moderately tense villain confrontation. Young children (under 5) might find Olivia Colman's villain reveal mildly scary.
- **Drug/Alcohol Content (None):** Nothing to report.
- **Positive Messages:** Family, kindness, good manners, overcoming greed, the value of chosen family, respecting your heritage while choosing your own path.

**For parents:** This is as safe as theatrical releases get. Worth It or Woke called it "shocking and beyond-refreshing" that there was nothing to flag. We agree. Take the whole family.

tropeAudit.name: Immigration/Refugee Subtext
tropeAudit.description: The Paddington franchise has always carried immigration subtext. A bear from 'Darkest Peru' arrives in London, is taken in by a kind British family, and proves himself through politeness and good behavior. In Peru, this is inverted: Paddington returns to his homeland and must decide whether to stay or go back to London. The subtext is present but never weaponized. It's organic to the character's origin story, not injected for political purposes.
tropeAudit.verdict: Minimal woke impact. Organic to character, not ideological payload.

tropeAudit.name: Bumbling Father Figure
tropeAudit.description: Henry Brown is portrayed as somewhat anxious and out of his depth during the adventure portions of the film. This is a mild version of the 'incompetent dad' trope that pervades family cinema. However, Henry redeems himself by stepping up in the climax and protecting his family. The arc is complete and positive.
tropeAudit.verdict: Minor woke trope, fully redeemed by the character's arc.

tropeAudit.name: Lack of Peruvian Representation
tropeAudit.description: A film set entirely in Peru features no notable Peruvian actors. Antonio Banderas is Spanish, Carla Tous is Colombian. Common Sense Media flagged this. However, this is a British franchise about a CGI bear, and the casting is star-driven rather than representation-driven. It cuts both ways: it avoids tokenism but also avoids authentic representation.
tropeAudit.verdict: Neutral. Neither woke nor anti-woke, just Hollywood casting.

tropeAudit.name: Female Villain With Male Accomplice Trope Inversion
tropeAudit.description: Olivia Colman's Clarissa Cabot is the film's true villain, with Antonio Banderas' Hunter serving as her unwitting pawn. This inverts the more traditional male-villain dynamic. However, Colman is so entertaining in the role that the gender dynamic feels irrelevant. She's a great villain because she's a great actress chewing scenery, not because the filmmakers wanted to make a point about female villainy.
tropeAudit.verdict: Minor woke coding, overwhelmed by sheer entertainment value.

tropeAudit.name: Token Diversity in Background London Scenes
tropeAudit.description: The London neighborhood scenes include diverse background characters. This is consistent with the prior films and reflects modern London. Not forced, not foregrounded.

tropeAudit.name: Environmental/Nature Preservation Undertone
tropeAudit.description: El Dorado turns out to be a natural grove, not a city of gold. The film implicitly values nature and heritage over material wealth. This could be read as environmental messaging, but it's so gentle and embedded in the fairy tale structure that it barely registers as political.
tropeAudit.verdict: Barely detectable. Traditional values packaging, not progressive activism.

tropeAudit.name: Family Unity as Central Value
tropeAudit.description: The entire film is about family. The Browns travel to Peru together because family sticks together. Paddington's journey is about choosing his adopted family over his biological origins. Hunter Cabot's redemption comes from choosing his daughter over treasure. Every character arc resolves through family bonds. This is the film's beating heart and it's traditional to the bone.
tropeAudit.verdict: Core traditional value. The film's strongest and most sincere element.

tropeAudit.name: Chosen Family / Adoption Celebrated
tropeAudit.description: Paddington's climactic choice to return to London with the Browns, after reconnecting with his birth origins and the bears of El Dorado, is the film's most emotionally powerful moment. Adoption and chosen family are celebrated without qualification. This is not framed as second-best. It's framed as home.
tropeAudit.verdict: Strong traditional element. Adoption treated as beautiful, not compensatory.

tropeAudit.name: Good Manners and Kindness as Heroic Virtues
tropeAudit.description: Paddington's defining trait across all three films is his unfailing politeness, his belief in seeing the good in people, and his insistence on doing the right thing. In a cinematic landscape dominated by sarcasm and moral relativism, Paddington's earnest goodness is practically counter-cultural. He says 'please' and 'thank you.' He shares his marmalade. He forgives people who don't deserve it. This is the franchise's secret weapon and it remains fully intact in the third film.
tropeAudit.verdict: Powerfully traditional. Counter-cultural in its sincerity.

tropeAudit.name: Male Characters Redeemed Through Responsibility
tropeAudit.description: Henry Brown overcomes his anxiety to protect his family. Hunter Cabot overcomes his obsession with gold to save Paddington and reconcile with his daughter. Jonathan Brown learns the value of hard work. All three male characters have traditional redemption arcs that involve stepping up, taking responsibility, and putting others first.
tropeAudit.verdict: Solidly traditional. Men improve by embracing duty and selflessness.

tropeAudit.name: Respect for Elders and Heritage
tropeAudit.description: Aunt Lucy is treated with deep reverence. The entire adventure is motivated by Paddington's love and concern for his elderly aunt. The Home for Retired Bears is portrayed warmly. Mrs. Bird (Julie Walters) is the wise elder who sees through the villain's deception. Elders are respected, valued, and central to the story.
tropeAudit.verdict: Traditional. Elders are wise, loved, and worth traveling across the world for.

tropeAudit.name: Greed Punished / Materialism Rejected
tropeAudit.description: Both villains are motivated by greed for gold. Both are punished. Hunter is redeemed when he abandons his greed. Clarissa, who refuses to give up her gold obsession, is literally sent to the North Pole. El Dorado itself turns out to be a grove of orange trees, not gold. The message is clear and deeply traditional: love and family are the real treasure. Material wealth is an illusion that corrupts.
tropeAudit.verdict: Classic traditional morality tale. Greed destroys, love redeems.

reviewBody:
Paddington Bear has become one of the strangest cultural Rorschach tests in modern cinema. Progressives see him as an immigration parable: a brown-skinned refugee from a developing nation, taken in by a white British family, who proves his worth through politeness and hard work. Conservatives claimed him after Queen Elizabeth herself shared tea and marmalade sandwiches with the little bear in that 2022 Platinum Jubilee sketch, cementing Paddington as an icon of traditional British values, good manners, and institutional respect. Both readings have some truth. Neither captures the full picture.

Paddington in Peru, the third film in the franchise, sidesteps the debate entirely by doing what Paddington does best: being kind, being funny, and making you feel things. Director Dougal Wilson, stepping in for Paul King (who directed the first two films to 97% and 99% on Rotten Tomatoes), delivers a perfectly pleasant adventure that families will enjoy and forget within a week. It's charming. It's warm. It's also the weakest entry in the franchise by a meaningful margin, and the reasons have nothing to do with politics.

Paddington receives a letter from the Home for Retired Bears in Peru informing him that his beloved Aunt Lucy misses him terribly and has been acting strangely. Paddington and the entire Brown family pack up and head to Peru. When they arrive at the convent where Aunt Lucy lives, the Reverend Mother (Olivia Colman) informs them that Lucy has disappeared into the jungle, leaving behind only her glasses and a bracelet. Paddington discovers a map in Lucy's cabin pointing toward a mysterious place called Rumi Rock.

The Browns hire a riverboat captain named Hunter Cabot (Antonio Banderas) and his daughter Gina (Carla Tous) to take them downriver. Hunter is obsessed with finding El Dorado, the legendary lost city of gold, and sees Paddington's bracelet as the key to unlocking its location. His treasure fever eventually causes a shipwreck and separates Paddington from the family.

Meanwhile, back at the convent, Mrs. Bird (Julie Walters) grows suspicious of the Reverend Mother and discovers she's actually Clarissa Cabot, Hunter's supposedly dead cousin who staged Lucy's disappearance to lure Paddington to Peru. It's a reasonably clever twist, and Colman plays the villainess with obvious relish. She's not quite Hugh Grant's Phoenix Buchanan from Paddington 2, who remains one of the great comic villains of the decade, but she's entertaining enough.

The threads converge at an ancient Incan fortress. Clarissa reveals herself, holds the family at gunpoint, and is stopped by Hunter, who finally overcomes his gold obsession and chooses his daughter over fortune. The Browns use Paddington's bracelet to enter El Dorado, which turns out not to be a city of gold at all. It's an orangery: a hidden grove where Paddington was born and where bears have been making marmalade for generations. Lucy is safe. Paddington reconnects with his origins, bonds with the other bears, and then makes the choice that defines the film. He returns to London with the Browns. Home isn't where you're from. It's where your family is.

That's a beautiful message, and the film earns it honestly. No lectures. No winking at the camera about immigration policy. Just a bear choosing love.

Hugh Grant pops up in a post-credits scene reprising Phoenix Buchanan, and it's delightful. The man understood the assignment.

So is Paddington in Peru woke? Not really. It carries the franchise's inherent immigration subtext (a bear from "Darkest Peru" finds home in Britain), but the films have never weaponized this. It's baked into the source material from Michael Bond's 1958 novel, inspired by wartime evacuees, not by modern political talking points. The film's actual themes are relentlessly traditional: family first, kindness matters, greed corrupts, elders deserve respect, home is where love is.

The male characters get genuine arcs. Henry Brown starts as a slightly anxious dad, then mans up to protect his family in the jungle. Hunter Cabot overcomes his generational obsession with gold and reconciles with his daughter. Jonathan Brown, the lazy-but-brilliant son, learns the value of hard work. Worth It or Woke, a conservative review site, specifically praised these arcs and noted that the female characters' flaws amount to "being too hardworking and loving too much." That's a fair read.

The women are well-served too, just differently. Mary Brown (Emily Mortimer, replacing Sally Hawkins) is warm and competent. Mrs. Bird is the shrewdest character in the film, the one who sees through the villain's disguise. Olivia Colman's villain is funny and menacing on her own terms, not as a "girl boss" statement.

On casting: the film is set entirely in Peru but features very few Latin American actors in prominent roles. Antonio Banderas is Spanish. Carla Tous is Colombian (she replaced Rachel Zegler, who left during the SAG-AFTRA strike). Common Sense Media flagged the absence of Peruvian actors. It's a valid observation, though the franchise has never pretended to be a vehicle for Latin American representation. This is a British bear voiced by Ben Whishaw. Geographic authenticity was never the point.

The biggest issue with Paddington in Peru isn't ideological. It's quality. The transition from Paul King to Dougal Wilson is noticeable. Wilson, making his feature debut after a career in commercials and music videos, has a gorgeous visual eye. The Peruvian landscapes are stunning. The set pieces are inventive. But he lacks King's gift for precision comedy and pacing. The middle act sags under an overly complicated treasure hunt plot. The villain reveal, while entertaining, lacks the sustained comic genius of Grant's Buchanan. The film feels about fifteen minutes too long.

Paddington (2014) was a revelation: nobody expected a CGI bear movie to be one of the best comedies of the decade. Paddington 2 (2017) improved on it and held a perfect 100% on Rotten Tomatoes for a stretch. Paddington in Peru sits at 94% on RT and 6.6 on IMDB, which are strong numbers in isolation but represent a clear step down for the franchise. The film grossed $192 million worldwide against a $75-90 million budget, so it's a commercial success, but not the breakout the first two were.

Here's the bottom line for parents: this is one of the safest, cleanest, most family-friendly theatrical releases you'll find in 2025. No profanity. No sexual content. No drug references. Mild peril during the adventure sequences. Olivia Colman's villain turn might mildly frighten very young children (under 5), but that's the extent of it. Worth It or Woke called it "shocking and beyond-refreshing" that there was nothing to report on the content front. We agree.

Paddington in Peru won't convert anyone or start any arguments. It won't make you rethink your politics or challenge your worldview. It will make you smile, possibly tear up, and leave the theater feeling warm. The fact that this counts as remarkable in 2025 says more about the state of family cinema than it does about the film itself.

The bear is fine. The bear is always fine. We could all stand to be a little more like the bear.

VERDICT: MIXED (Leaning Traditional). Woke 8.4, Trad 22.5, Composite +14 TRAD.
